#3671. A Survivor of Alleged Sex Abuse at Miss Hall’s School in the Berkshires Speaks Out.

At 6:04 on the morning of March 29, 2024, my phone lit up with a long text from Matt Rutledge. The head of school had called him the night before, he wrote, while he was watching television with his wife. He was on paid administrative leave, his school email was frozen, and he assumed this was about him and me. He called what he had done to me a relationship. He didn’t regret his feelings for me. Could I call him when his wife was out of the house?

I was thirty-seven years old. I was a few weeks out from my partnership interview at a New York law firm. I had a husband and a three-year-old son. I spend my working life telling clients which sentences will look bad in discovery. I read that text twice, and my first thought was, How can I help him?

He had spent years teaching me to use his word for it. It was never a relationship. He groomed me, he exploited me, and he raped me.

Vanity Fair has written about that morning before. Evgenia Peretz opened “Girls, Interrupted” with that text in January 2025, and she went back to Miss Hall’s last fall after the investigation came out. In March, Dan Adler covered the indictment. This time I’m telling it myself.

Later that morning an email arrived from an attorney in Boston. Subject line: “Reaching out about Miss Hall’s School.” I didn’t open it right away. I didn’t need to. Some part of me had been composing that email in my head since I was a teenager. The attorney represented a woman named Melissa Fares, a Miss Hall’s alumna who had been there a few years after me. I had never heard her name.

She had heard mine. Years earlier, older girls at the school had told her about me. She held on to my name, and when she went to a lawyer she remembered it. By then I had married and changed it, and they found me anyway.

I called Matt and asked. “Who is Melissa?” There was a pause long enough to hear him decide something, then a sigh, and then he told me he had had sex with Melissa while she was a student.

Here is what I did next, and I’d ask you to withhold judgment. I told him I would call the lawyer, find out what she had, and report back.

That’s what twenty-two years of being groomed looks like at a desk in Midtown. You don’t make a decision. The decision was made for you a long time ago, in a dorm room, and you’re simply carrying it out.

I did call the lawyer. And when I heard my own voice say “I’m not ready to talk to you, I want to talk to Melissa,” I think that was the first sentence in two decades that I said entirely for myself.

Melissa called that afternoon. I don’t remember how she started. I remember what I said before she got far.

“I’ve been waiting for your call for twenty years.”

I meant it literally. Some part of me had always known I wasn’t the only one. I just couldn’t go looking. I could only wait to be found.

Hilary Simon and Melissa Fares, photographed in Far Rockaway, New York, 2025.

She told me her story, and I heard my own memories come out of a stranger’s mouth. He called her “Little One.” He called me “Little One.” He took her to the same hotel in Northampton. He told her he would kill himself if she ever told anyone, which is a thing he had also told me, more than once, in nearly the same words. He had made himself the center of her emotional world before he ever touched her. He had a script.

For twenty years he had me believing that what happened was singular, and that it was my fault. By the end of that call it was a pattern, and I was a data point. I was not special. It is a strange thing to grieve, not being special to the person who hurt you. I grieved it anyway.

After more than three decades teaching at that school, he resigned the same day.

I arrived at Miss Hall’s, an all-girls boarding school in Pittsfield, Massachusetts, in the fall of 2001. I was fourteen, homesick, and like every other girl my age, positive I was more grown up than I was.

Rutledge had been teaching history there for a decade. He was a big man with a booming voice, married with two daughters. He lived with his family in a school-owned house across the street from the main entrance. He used to cut the lunch line announcing himself as “Mr. Wonderful.” Girls talked about him like he was a minor deity. They also mentioned, in the breezy way teenagers mention terrible things, that he had a type.

Some evenings, he was one of the adults who did bed checks in the dorms. The others always stood in the doorway. He came in and sat on the edge of my bed.

By the next fall he was my advisor and my cross-country coach. There was no door at that school he couldn’t open. On the long drives to meets, he told me to sit next to him in the school van. He called me his copilot. The rest of the team sat behind us. He would put his hand on my upper thigh, or pull me close until our legs were touching. I watched the Berkshire hills go by and tried not to look down.

That was the first line he crossed. I was fifteen. After that he crossed them one at a time until there were none left. He kept abusing me for years after I graduated.

From the outside, those years looked like a success story.

I went to college and then law school. I became a civil defense attorney. I got married. I had a son. I was good at my job.

I could find the unanswered email in ten thousand pages of discovery. The report nobody followed up on. I couldn’t open my own file.

When I tell this story, people ask me some version of the same question. How did nobody notice?

In the late 1990s, years before I ever set foot on Miss Hall’s campus, a student stood up at a school meeting and said Mr. Rutledge was having sex with another student. The school suspended her for the rest of the year, barred her from graduation and made her write him an apology letter. He kept teaching.

On my graduation day, Rutledge kissed me and told me that he loved me. A classmate told a staff member, who reported it to the administration. In a memo, Rutledge admitted telling me he loved me but said “[it was] not a romantic expression.” He denied the kiss. They took his word for it. No one called me or my parents.

A few years later, after a family reported that he had made advances toward their daughter, the head of school at that time, Jeannie Norris, put a warning to Rutledge in writing. “This isn’t the 70s or the 80s,” she wrote. “Society has no stomach for any kind of inappropriate behavior between adults and girls or teachers and students.” She was worried about the school’s reputation, and about his. In the letter she said the incident had “the potential for seriously damaging the School and your [Rutledge’s] reputation.” He was not fired.

Over the years that followed Rutledge was made chair of the history department and collected faculty honors. More than one person gave the school my name as a girl he had singled out. Nobody ever called me. In June 2023, I heard another alumna tried to raise concerns about him with the head of school at that time. He was still teaching nine months later, when Melissa reported him.

In August 2025 Miss Hall’s published the results of an outside investigation it had commissioned from Aleta Law. The investigators substantiated grooming and abuse by Rutledge involving at least five students. They found school leadership had been warned about him over the years and hadn’t acted. Staff members told investigators they had suspected him and kept quiet, some because they feared retaliation, others because they assumed no one in charge would listen.

It went beyond Rutledge. The investigation found that seven other Miss Hall’s employees had engaged in sexual misconduct with students, dating back to the 1940s. Eight adults across eighty plus years. That’s a culture of abuse.

A Berkshire County grand jury has since indicted Norris on a charge of reckless endangerment of a child. She has pleaded not guilty. Another former Miss Hall’s teacher has been indicted for assault with intent to rape and indecent assault and two counts battery of a student. He has also pleaded not guilty.

I read all sixty pages of the Aleta Law report in one sitting. Nothing in it surprised me. It still knocked the air out of me to see my adolescence reduced to numbered findings.

Melissa arrived at Miss Hall’s in 2007, two years after I left.

People sometimes call us friends. That’s true, but it’s a small word for it. I call her my sister survivor.

I wouldn’t be writing this if Melissa hadn’t gone first. She went to the school alone. In April 2024, she told her story publicly. A few weeks later, I told mine. Then other women came forward. They said Rutledge had abused them too.

In October 2024, the Berkshire district attorney said he didn’t believe he could charge Rutledge. In Massachusetts, the age of consent is sixteen. Under the law, a teacher could claim that a sixteen- or seventeen-year-old student had consented.

Melissa and I set out to change the law. We testified at the State House and knocked on every door that would open. Enough Abuse, a Massachusetts nonprofit, had been fighting for this for years. Two national advocacy groups, World Without Exploitation and I Have The Right To, stood with us. Representatives Leigh Davis and John Lawn pushed for it in the House, and Senator Joan Lovely added it to the state budget. In July, Governor Healey signed the Trusted Adults Act.

In Massachusetts, it is now a felony for a teacher or coach to have sex with a student under eighteen.

Melissa and I spoke at the signing ceremony. I stood right next to the governor and thought about the girl in the front seat of the school van, with her teacher’s hand on her leg.

While we were working on the law, Massachusetts State Police and a new team of prosecutors in the Berkshire district attorney’s office had reopened the investigation into Rutledge. Melissa and I testified before a grand jury. In March, he was indicted on three counts of rape.

In April, he was arraigned. It was the first time Melissa and I faced him together. In the courtroom, I handed out orange heart stickers. Orange is Melissa’s favorite color. When we saw Rutledge, we both went numb. We had learned to do that as girls, when going somewhere else in our heads was the only way through. He pleaded not guilty.

I looked back at the benches. They were full of orange. Teachers from Miss Hall’s, people from the community, alumnae across generations. I had been alone with this since I was fifteen. That day, a whole room sat behind us. Afterward, Melissa told reporters that for the first time, she held the power in a room with him. I felt it too.

This month, nine years after #MeToo took off, a jury in London convicted Russell Brand of one rape and three sexual assaults. A judge sentenced him to ten and a half years in prison. His crimes went back to 2004. Brand’s attorneys argued the women had waited too long to be believed. I waited twenty years. Delay is often the most ordinary fact in these cases.

In the midterms, Ohio elected Amy Acton governor. A few weeks before the vote, her opponent’s campaign ran an ad in which her estranged mother called her a liar. Acton’s stepfather had been charged with raping her when she was a child. Republicans and Democrats both condemned the ad. She won anyway.

I watched the returns on election night and thought about the girls at Miss Hall’s who told the truth and were called liars. Survivors get called liars all the time. We almost never get to watch one win.

Tarana Burke knew survivors weren’t being believed long before most people were listening. She started saying “me too” in 2006 to reach Black girls who had survived sexual violence, more than ten years before it became a hashtag. Every survivor who spoke after her made it a little easier for the next one.

In November 2024, a Cornell student told campus police and the Title IX office that she had been gang-raped at a fraternity house weeks earlier. No one has been charged. Cornell’s president set up a task force on sexual assault, but he later admitted he never checked how her case ended.

When I read that, I was back at Miss Hall’s on graduation day, waiting for a phone call that nobody made.

The Epstein survivors know that silence too. For decades, powerful people looked away. Last year survivors pushed Congress to pass a law requiring the Justice Department to release its Epstein files. Millions of pages came out. There have been no arrests in the United States.

I’m still hopeful. Survivors everywhere keep coming forward, and some of the people in charge are finally acting. My body knew what Rutledge had done to me long before I let myself say it aloud. I didn’t have the words. Survivors today do, and they have each other. Melissa found me.

The criminal case against Rutledge isn’t over. His lawyer has asked a judge to dismiss all charges. We don’t know yet whether there will be a trial. Whatever the judge decides, I’ve already reached my own verdict. I’m healing and Rutledge doesn’t get a say in that.

For most of my life, I carried shame that was never mine. He handed it to me. Every adult who looked away handed me a little more.

Predators don’t work alone. Someone always sees something. In the movie Spotlight, a lawyer says that if it takes a village to raise a child, it takes a village to abuse one. My village saw. The people in charge did nothing.

I’ve given the shame back. It belongs to him, and to the people who could have stopped him.

If you are a survivor and you are still carrying shame, you can put it down.

Borrow my courage if you need it. Melissa lent me hers.

Neither Matthew Rutledge nor Jean Norris responded to Vanity Fair for the original story, and neither of them has made direct statements to the press. Norris, through her attorney, claimed not to know that Rutledge abused students.

While Avalancheâs in-house bruiser is willing to operate outside of the confines of the law, the same cannot be said of her merchandising. According to Chinese media [and caught by Automaton Media], Shanghai police have arrested 13 individuals in connection to a bootleg toy operation, who oddly enough specialized in unlicensed dolls of Final Fantasy 7âs Tifa Lockhart.

Shanghai authorities began their investigation in May of this year. Purchasers of a figure based on Lockhartâs negligee appearance at the Honey Bee Inn were disappointed to discover what they received was not quite as advertised. While resembling the merchandise from Play Arts, Square Enixâs in-house toymaker, closer inspection revealed the goods were made of different material, had more simplistic attire and a lack of poseable articulation points. While some might shy away from flagging the cops about such specific buying habits, enough complaints came in to launch further inquiry.

Police have arrested 13 people accused of selling counterfeit Final Fantasy 7 Tifa Lockhart figures

The Chinese sellers reportedly charged higher prices by including extra faces, hands, and accessories not found with the official figures pic.twitter.com/AE1IyS0wi9

In collaboration with the rights holders, police discovered an online network of unauthorized vendors using group chats and digital marketplaces to circulate the inauthentic merch. The ring of counterfeiters allegedly hired the services of a factory in Guangzhou to produce the goods. Police say the operation generated over 2 million yuan (approximately $300,000 USD) and had been selling the knock-offs since 2024. It is hardly an isolated incident. Like all recent collection frenzies, demand for upper-scale figurines of video game and anime characters has risen rapidly around the globe. GamesRadar says that this year alone, Shanghai police have arrested more than 140 individuals and confiscated over ten million dollars worth of bootleg play things.

Fix the '70 Riata by tracking down some wrecked cars.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

You'll have to track down the GTA 6 Riata locations to fix the second Classic Car Collection vehicle for Wyman. He'll text you a little while after you complete the Transgressor, this time sending you to the Key Lento area, unfortunately a rather long drive when you're likely still at the motel near Port Gellhorn.

There are three Riatas you need to scan with the WAink It app to fix up this classic off-roading 4x4, one in Key Lento itself, one near the naval base at Goose Key, and a final one in Shoeless Keys.

This is the first one Wyman asks you to find, near the PD in the Keys. It's under a brown stilt house north of Leonida Key Lento Mini-mart and the Shrimp 'n Save, on that northernmost road running through the Key. Find the brown stilt house, as in the video above, then just head underneath to scan the car.

This second one is located in Southwind, on Goose Key, the island with the Mile Zero Air Station to the west of Key Lento—you will have visited here for a mission early in the game. The junked car is under another brown stilt house at the end of the road down to the east from the Xero Gas - Southwind station, on the right just before the sea.

This third one is located behind the ruined gas station just to the north of Grassrivers Cafe & Deli in Shoeless Keys. The tricky part is that this is a four-star area (because of the final missions in Chapter 1), so you'll want to be quick as otherwise a police chopper will come and spot you. When you turn off the main road, the garage is on your left before you reach the cafe itself, with the car just behind.

Somehow, I forgot to record this one, but I still show the location in the clip above behind the gas station (just without the car since it was gone when I re-recorded).

Once you have all three, Wyman will tell you to wait a little while, and then will call and ask you to Buck him $1,500 for the labour. Select the payment request in the text, or do it manually in the app. A little while after the money is sent, you'll get a map marker for Wyman's scrapyard, where you can pick up this completed classic car.

#3668. New Scientific Analysis Suggests Jeffrey Epstein Was Murdered. His Brother, For One, Feels Validated.

One day in August 2019, Mark Epstein was having breakfast at a Virginia hotel when he looked at the TV and saw CNN reporting that his older brother, Jeffrey Epstein, had died by suicide in a Manhattan federal prison. As jarring as the news was, he had no reason to doubt it.

“I knew he wouldn’t want to live the rest of his life in jail,” Mark told Vanity Fair this week. “He had no children to worry about. Our parents were gone. He knew he didn’t have to worry about me.”

Mark says he finished his omelet and headed back to New York. Then, like so many other Americans, he started to become skeptical of the official narrative.

Over the last seven years, the endless conspiracy theories surrounding Jeffrey Epstein’s death have largely been relegated to the backwaters of YouTube and Reddit, while local and federal authorities have stuck to the suicide story. But this week there was a breakthrough. On Monday, Michael Freeman, a leading forensic scientist who testified for the prosecution in the trial of Derek Chauvin for the murder of George Floyd, issued the most legitimate challenge to date to the prevailing consensus.

Freeman presented his findings at a historic London legal society, saying, “The pattern and distribution and multitude of injuries are not explained by a suicidal hanging.” In a New York Times story published the same day as the presentation, Freeman told the paper that he had no view on who might have killed Jeffrey: “All I’m interested in is, how did this get so sideways?” Along with several global news organizations, including CBS and the BBC, the Times covered the development with a straight face even as it noted that Freeman’s efforts to publish his findings in a peer-reviewed journal had thus far been rejected.

The relationship between Donald Trump and Jeffrey Epstein has loomed large over the president’s second term.

In his thick Brooklyn accent, Mark Epstein, who has long been trying to prove that his brother was murdered while awaiting trial on sex trafficking charges, excitedly recounted this milestone over the phone the day after Freeman’s presentation, which he attended.

“This crosses all party lines,” Mark said. “Most people believe he didn’t commit suicide. So it’s a mystery. People want an answer to that. I think now they have the answer.”

Mark emphasized that the story of the recent findings was not about him but rather about his brother’s death and Freeman’s work. It was Freeman who reached out to him, Mark said, based on what the scientist independently thought was shoddy work on Jeffrey’s autopsy, and Mark agreed to turn over all the records, reports, and photographs he had as next of kin.

“I want to make it really clear,” he said. “I didn’t pay for this. He’s never asked me for anything other than the information, which I gave him willingly. And he’s been studying this. As a matter of fact, the night before last was the first time I ever met him face-to-face.”

Still, Mark has made his suspicions both his calling card and his personal mission in recent years. After working in real estate investing and serving as the chair of Cooper Union’s board of trustees, he had his own business dealings come under some scrutiny as Jeffrey’s life and crimes dominated political and cultural discourse beginning in the late 2010s—Jeffrey allegedly housed models and employees in an Upper East Side building that was predominantly owned by his brother’s real estate holding company. In the years since his brother’s death, Mark has said that Jeffrey “definitely had dirt” on Donald Trump, and he became a minor fixation amid the Epstein files rollout on account of emails containing banter between him and his brother. (Trump has denied any prior knowledge of Jeffrey’s crimes and said that the release of the Epstein files “totally exonerated” him.) Mark has dismissed a suicide note purportedly written by Jeffrey as a fabrication.

Jeffrey’s death certificate initially said “pending further study” in regard to the cause of death, rather than ruling it a homicide or suicide, but the chief medical examiner ruled it a suicide days later. “All the pathologists I’ve spoken to,” says Mark, “they said, [if] an initial death certificate says ‘pending further study,’ you don’t get an answer usually for weeks or more because something’s being studied.” Mark hired the celebrity forensic pathologist Michael Baden to observe and evaluate the autopsy, and Baden previously stated that “the evidence points to homicide.” Federal officials’ handling of the matter in the years to come only amplified Mark’s concern.

“You know a suicide when you see one,” FBI director Kash Patel said last year while he was under fire for not producing any proof of the Epstein conspiracies he had been touting during his time as a mere conservative podcast personality, “and that’s what that was.”

“I actually laughed out loud when I heard that,” Mark said, “because I thought, How many suicides has this fucking jackass actually seen?”

So who does Mark think killed his brother?

“It’s like in a Mob hit,” he said. “You try to find who the hit man was, and then you try to find who ordered the hit.” The hit man, he figured, could only be someone among a limited number of people: prison employees and other prisoners who had been on Jeffrey’s security tier. “Then the question becomes,” said Mark, “who would have the ability to orchestrate this in a federal prison, and who would have the ability to have the DOJ cover it up?” He couldn’t think of anyone besides Trump. (Trump has not been accused of any wrongdoing in connection to Jeffrey’s death; in a 2023 interview with Tucker Carlson, when asked whether Jeffrey could have been killed, he said, “Oh sure, it’s possible. I mean, I don’t really believe—I think he probably committed suicide.”)

I thought Mark and I had developed some rapport over the conversation, particularly after I mentioned that I’d attended the same Coney Island middle school where he and his brother had been students; I emphasized that I was trying to listen to him carefully and take him seriously. But there was a bit more rancor in his tone after I said it was still difficult to believe that the Department of Justice could have successfully covered up the murder of the most high-profile prisoner in the world.

“If you don’t think that after what I just told you,” Mark said, “then you, sir, are a fucking idiot also.”

#3667. Binding Of Isaac Update Review-Bombed Over AI-Generated Music In GTA 6 Mode: ‘Woke Up To A Sh*t Show, Obviously I Had No Idea’

AIGTA 6NicalisSoundtrackSteamThe Binding of Isaac: Repentance+

The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+ was a free update to the beloved roguelike that arrived on PC in 2024, but launched on console earlier this week in a head-to-head matchup against Grand Theft Auto 6. The marketing stunt may have been a success, but AI-generated music tracks discovered in a special new Vice City mode have turned the launch into a nightmare.

While Repentance+ came to PS5, Xbox Series X/S, and Switch 2 this week, the Steam version of the game also got a free update. “Be sure to get in and play today’s Daily Run for a very special crime-packed surprise. Enter the Basement, and go out in a glorious blaze of bullets and vehicular homicide!” read the patch notes on on Valve’s storefront. Players could enter the seed “V1CE BSMT” into the roguelike before starting their run to launch a GTA-inspired version with special weapons and music.

Earlier today, however, Reddit user ShweetsStuff posted a comprehensive breakdown of the new music tracks alleging they were made with Suno, an AI-based music generation tool. “The new update includes 14 music files for the run; seven full songs, plus some derivatives (intros/outros),” the wrote. The post continued:

Some include Suno metadata with them. You can find this information yourself by just checking the file comment metadata (something common like VLC has tools for this, but here’s ffprobe output of drivingsong1.ogg, for example):

comment : made with suno; created=2026-10-30T17:53:41Z; id=cd5a5b55-bead-4cb9-949d-09ed1f917dce

Other files have this comment scrubbed; they were edited/exported later, but nonetheless there’s the proof.

Please report issues and bugs to the email attached. https://t.co/KHKSqKGsUe

— ð Edmund McMillen ð (@edmundmcmillen) November 21, 2026

“They’ve had how long now to prepare the GTA 6 release Easter egg daily run literally nobody asked for and still ai slopped it? Are you fucking kidding me,” one fan wrote on the Binding of Isaac subreddit. “No shit, itâs 2026. The entire industry is like this. Cutting corners constantly because they know they can get away with it,” wrote another.

Many have blamed Nicalis, the publisher and co-developer of the Repentance+ expansion, in particular. Complaints about ongoing bugs, latency, and quality control issues have seemingly been building for some time. The latest mishap results in a review-bomb of the expansion’s Steam page, which currently sits at an abysmal user rating of just 9 percent positive. “AI generated music in GTA mode; Edmund please take back control of the game,” reads one of the latest Steam reviews. “Not to mention there’s like single digit bug fixes in a year+ long awaited update with no other changes.”

The AI music was news to Edmund McMillen, the game’s creator. “Woke up to a shit show, obviously I had no idea it featured generated music in the daily run, looking into how that happened and getting it removed, stay tuned,” he posted earlier today on X. An emergency update has since gone out to remove the AI-generated music as well as address some other versions with the latest version of the expansion, but Nicalis has yet to take responsibility for the use of AI or explained how it made it into the game.

Steam requires store page disclosures for any content that uses assets generated with the help of AI, which The Binding of Isaac: Repentance+Â did not have, despite the big publicity push around the latest update and it landing on the same day as Rockstar’s open-world blockbuster. “That was [Nicalis’] idea,” McMillen recently told Eurogamer. “‘Wouldn’t it be funny if…?’ I was like, whatever, that’s funny…We’re done, so we’ve got to release this month…It’s a fun experiment.”

It turns out Elizabeth Holmes’ partner, Billy Evans, did successfully manage a payout from the producers of You Can See Everything, which has been crushing it on the 2026 movie schedule. However, the money isn’t going to him or Holmes. Instead, it’s going to charity. The details are still a little murky, but we do have more understanding of what went down after the scene in the movie where he brings it up and the card at the end that explains he changed his mind and wasn’t going to profit from the movie. Given how big a box office hit ($89 million and counting) the A24 release has been, it's probably a nice chunk of change. So what is going on? Here’s what we know.

One of the more controversial aspects of the production of You Can See Everything was Evans negotiating a payout with execs from A24 and the movie's co-directors, Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim. The scene, which sees Evans asking for money after Holmes has left the room, has been a topic of conversation among fans of the film. Even lawyers have chimed in on how it could affect the judgment against Holmes, who owes somewhere north of $400 million in restitution after her conviction on fraud crimes.

In the scene, everyone agrees that Evans (and presumably Holmes) will be paid for their appearances. Then, at the end, a card appears informing the audience that Evans backed off this deal and wouldn’t be paid. Now, a new report in The Hollywood Reporter has clarified it. According to the article, Evans is earning money on the backend, but that money is reportedly going to a children’s charity. The article did not specify which charity.

The outlet also confirmed with A24 that a deal had been struck, but neither the outlet’s sources nor A24 revealed how much the charity would be getting or what percentage of the backend was negotiated. The film is closing in on $100 million at the box office, and it's sure to earn more when it hits VOD sometime in the near future (the exact date is still not confirmed). That’s to say nothing about whatever money the film will earn when it moves to HBO Max, likely in early 2027.

This is yet another saga in a movie that is full of intrigue both on-screen and off. It is also another wrinkle in trying to determine what is true and what is not. That question is at the core of the movie, and it seems even now, weeks after its release and years after Evans and Holmes were filmed before she reported to prison in 2023. That question is still lingering in every aspect. I’ve said before that this movie is like an onion, and this is one more layer getting peeled away, but it’s only offering up another layer that is just as fascinating.

#3665. Jenny McCarthy Recalls Getting 'Cheap' Breast Augmentation at 19

Jenny McCarthy is getting candid about her previously botched breast augmentation procedure.

“This was back when I was living on the south side of Chicago and all of my girlfriends were going to Arizona to get this boob job that was on sale for $1,500,” McCarthy, 54, recalled on the Thursday, November 19, episode of her eponymous podcast. “They would come back with the most gorgeous freaking cleavage you’d ever seen. Growing up as an athlete and not having a lot of meat on my bones, I craved boobs.”

Following in her friends’ footsteps, a then-19-year-old McCarthy “saved up” her money to get her own procedure.

“I go to Arizona, I do the appointment. He’s like, ‘OK.’ I tell him, ‘I just want small C’s just so they’re not that noticeable.’ I go in for the surgery. I’m very, very nervous,” she said of the plastic surgeon. “Halfway through the surgery, I wake up on the table and I literally say to the doctor, ‘Um, I’m awake.’ And he goes, ‘Oh, yeah. Well, we’ve got just one more boob to go.’”

McCarthy was admittedly “freaking out” that the anesthesia allegedly wore off before the second implant was even surgically placed in her chest.

“He’s like, ‘Just hang out, just chill. You’ll be fine.’ I remember him saying, “You won’t remember a thing.’ I remember everything, buddy,” she quipped. “Now I know why it was so cheap ‘cause they didn’t put us to sleep!”

McCarthy continued, “During a boob job surgery, I had no idea they did this, but once they put the implants in, they press a button … and the table rises you up to a standing position, and all of the doctors and nurses go to the other side of the room and they go and they’re literally examining you from across the room to see if you’re even.”

Since McCarthy was awake, the examination was especially terrifying.

“Now, this would be fine if you’re asleep right now. Imagine you were me, OK? I’m standing there strapped to the table like this having these people stare at me to see if it’s even,” she said. “I wanted to go home so bad. I’m like, ‘This was the biggest mistake of my life.’”

Once the surgery was over, the Masked Singer panelist also had a difficult recovery.

“I am throwing up everywhere,” McCarthy said. “I was never in so much pain in my entire life because I felt the pain during the surgery. It made it a hundred times worse afterwards. … I should have known something was different when I was driven through a back alley for the entrance.”

#3664. At Chanel’s Dinner, Party Talk Turns to Fashion Gossip and Classic Literature, as Guests Sparkle In House Diamonds

“That is the highest compliment you could give anyone!” Lux Pascal says after I tell her she looks like Jessica Paré’s Megan Draper from Mad Men. We’re at Chanel’s Watches and Fine Jewelry holiday dinner, held at Daniel Humm’s new eponymous restaurant, Humm, in the West Village. Pascal is in a ’60s black modish leather minidress that she’s paired with a cat eye. On her wrists are Chanel’s Première Galon watch and Coco Crush bracelets, which, like her rings and earrings, are all dotted with diamonds. As I look around, most of the celebrities dressed by the brand are wearing looks that show off their French fine accessories. Ella Rubin, the Gen Z star of the hit teen TV show Sterling Point, has upgraded a simple pair of vintage Levi’s with a sleek black-and-gold Première Ribbon watch and several diamond rings. This is not a night for hidden gems.

The Pierre Yovanovitch–designed restaurant is a verified New York power room at the moment: There’s Derek Blasberg talking to Sarah Pidgeon about books—War and Peace gets a name-check—and Architectural Digest’s Amy Astley in a corner with Metropolitan Museum of Art board member Robert Denning. Indrė Rockefeller is here, as is stylist Vanessa Traina. In a feat of fun seating arrangements, the Chanel team has sat Rubin next to another young Ella: Beatty, the recent star of Monster and daughter of Warren Beatty and Annette Bening. (Although, with all due respect to those lovely Ellas, the two neighbors I’d most like to eavesdrop on are Devon Lee Carlson and Jack Harlow.) At the bar I hear two fashion people gossiping about industry hiring rumors: “Lauren Sherman says there’s two people in the running,” they whisper about some gig. I think I know what they’re talking about, but not enough to print it.

Laura Love and Devon Lee Carlson on November 17, 2026, in New York City (Photo by Dimitrios Kambouris/WireImage)

Guests mill about because there’s much to mill about: Humm’s filled his restaurant with dozens of notable, site-specific artworks. Louise Bourgeois supplied 24 watercolor paintings, as well as a fantastical sterling silver cast of one of her sculptures, situated by the bar. (Tonight it’s serving mezcal sours with guava and an apple brandy highball.) Francesco Clemente painted not one, not two, but four celestial murals across two months, with motifs of abstract stars, animals, trains, and clocks. On the walls in the main dining room are 12 pigment drawings by Roni Horn. Then there’s all the work by Rashid Johnson: In the lounge—which for this event doubles as a red carpet—hangs his painting Untitled Homes. With Yovanovitch, he also built a custom host stand cast in aluminum and painted red. It’s so textural that you can see the fingerprints, and a number of guests gather around it as the maître d’ explains Johnson’s artistic process like he’s a docent at The Met.

Chanel has decorated the tables with long taper candles and arrangements of deep fuchsia peonies and burgundy garden roses. Waiters serve Humm’s signature everything caviar bagels. When I think about ordering something other than the chicken, a waiter tells me not to. He’s right.

At the end of the night, after most guests are a few glasses of red wine (or martinis) deep, Pidgeon herself grabs a microphone. The event, as it turns out, has a surprise performer: girlsweetvoiced. “She captures something that’s very honest,” Pidgeon says of the emerging singer-songwriter, who then belts out a cover of Joni Mitchell’s “California.” Title aside, it’s been a very New York night.

#3661. Robert Pattinson Is the New James Bond—Revisit 007’s Style Legacy Here

There must be no male character across film history who has done more for menswear—and for the suit—than Bond, James Bond.

That is in part because the sartorial premise of Bond, the suave British spy, is remarkably simple: Presumably, all it takes to embody 007 is a black tuxedo, a sexy watch, and a pair of well-buffed dress shoes. And yet, as Daniel Craig, Pierce Brosnan, Sean Connery, and other dangerously handsome men have proven, a mere suit does not a 007 make. This is why, despite Bond being one of the most popular film characters of all time, you will rarely see ordinary men dare to take him on as a Halloween costume. There’s simply more to making Bond than a good tux.

Denis Villeneuve is set to direct the next era of the franchise, now under the creative control of Amazon MGM, and Robert Pattinson has been chosen to reincarnate the character conceived by Ian Fleming in 1953. In the announcement clip for Pattinson’s casting, the actor looks the part in a black tuxedo and white shirt, but it’s his eyes, which pierce through the camera rather than down the barrel of his gun, that do most of the talking and offer a suggestion of what Pattinson’s Bond may have to offer. Will he be a little darker and tortured, like his take on Batman? Or perhaps his Bond will be louche and somewhat pricklier.

A safer bet to make is that he will look good. One of the most enduring legacies of the James Bond franchise is how stylish both the character of Bond and the universe built around him have always been. Bond has appeared classic and timeless in style during each of the franchise’s eras, but hindsight offers a much richer perspective.

Pierce Brosnan, The World Is Not Enough, 1999.

As portrayed through the decades in the property’s famous title sequence, Bond is a silhouette—a classic, timeless silhouette. Fleming established the look in his development of the character when he made the suit his primary uniform. But it is Terence Young, the director of the first 007 films, who is responsible for the visual definition of Bond.

When Connery was cast as Bond for the first film, Dr. No (1962), Young, an avid wearer of suits himself, took him to his own tailor, Anthony Sinclair. We can credit Sinclair with developing the original silver screen Bond look: The suit was lighter in fit and tailoring than most other English suits at the time. The Bond suit had a soft shoulder and waist, but a strong, wide chest and a low button stance that elongated its wearer. Every Bond suit that’s followed has been measured to the standard of Sinclair’s work, and every Bond actor has had to compete with Connery’s charisma while wearing it.

Brosnan and his Brioni suits were indicative of the 1990s corporate look of the time. Craig wore Brioni too, but only for Casino Royale; Tom Ford created his subsequent suiting, which often stood out for the slim fit popular in the 2010s. Most memorable sartorially is Roger Moore’s take through the ’70s and ’80s, which often deviated from the sleekness that had come to define Bond by creating a little frisson with lighter, brighter fabrics and a bolder sense of playfulness.

The character of Bond, and the actor personifying him at a given time, have also become representative of a certain male standard: Connery in the ’60s, tan and athletic, or Brosnan in the ’90s, polished with lithe elegance. And then came Craig, whose casting was met with skepticism, to put it lightly. His arrival was marked by the image of the actor walking out of the ocean in tight swim trunks in Casino Royale. His strong legs, rounded shoulders, and sculpted, hairless chest cemented then and there the idea of what a leading man had become and would look like for the next two decades.

Daniel Craig as James Bond, Casino Royale, 2006.

Also synonymous with Bond are his watch and many vehicles. Most recently, Bond cars have all been made by Aston Martin, though Brosnan drove some spectacular BMWs. The official Bond timepiece since Brosnan’s turn has been Omega. But before such kinds of commercial partnerships were commonplace in Hollywood, Connery wore watches by Rolex, Gruen, and Breitling, while Moore wore pieces by Seiko.

With the news that Pattinson is taking on the mantle, an equally pressing question emerges: Who will be the first new Bond girl?

Some of the most memorable moments in the franchise’s history have been anchored by women. Halle Berry’s emergence from the ocean in an orange bikini and a white belt safekeeping a knife was only made better by the fact that this moment was an homage to the first Bond girl, Ursula Andress, and her ivory two-piece featuring a belt for her own weapon. Then there was Eva Green as Vesper Lynd in a slinky Versace dress in Casino Royale. But it didn’t get better than Grace Jones in A View to a Kill. As May Day, a fabulous femme fatale, Jones wore costumes designed for her by Azzedine Alaïa. How could anyone measure up?

Halle Berry and Pierce Brosnan, Die Another Day, 2002.

Roger Moore and Grace Jones, 1985, A View To a Kill, 1985.

Of course, we will have to see how stylistic choices play out in the 26th Bond film, which, like Bond movies of the past, will become emblematic of the era in which we live. It will also, as a creative project, have to contend with the way Hollywood operates today. The fact that Amazon now has full creative control over the franchise—the company acquired MGM, a co-owner of the Bond franchise rights, for $8.45 billion in 2022 and later struck a deal with the other co-owners in regard to creative authority—is the primary indication of that.

Pattinson will also be the first Bond with airtight fashion-brand deals. Craig was an Omega ambassador as an extension of his role as Bond, which made him a household name, and the 007s who came before him operated within a film industry that was not as closely connected to fashion.

Also unlike his predecessors, Pattinson is stepping into the role as a bona fide movie star who has appeared in three other major franchises (Harry Potter, Twilight, and Batman). He’s already one of the most prolific and bankable stars of his generation, and an undeniable part of being a movie star today is becoming the face of a franchise, a brand, or a product.

In September, Pattinson was announced as a global ambassador for Jaeger-LeCoultre, a Swiss watchmaker. But 007 has worn Omega watches onscreen for decades, a partnership between the brand and the franchise that dates back to the Brosnan years. If Omega’s partnership with the franchise remains for this new installment, it could present a potential conflict if Pattinson’s contract with Jaeger stipulates that he is not allowed to wear another brand’s watch onscreen or front related campaigns for competitors. It may sound like a banal preoccupation, as Pattinson has only just been cast, but there are millions of dollars at play, and actors today often make as much money from brand deals as they do from their turns onscreen.

Pattinson has also been an ambassador for Dior since 2013, serving first as a fragrance ambassador and subsequently as a face for ready-to-wear Dior Homme; he was originally tapped under Kris Van Assche, with his ambassadorship extending through Kim Jones’s tenure at the renamed Dior Men and now continuing with Jonathan Anderson at the helm of the French mega-brand. Will Anderson be providing his suits? The Irish designer has costumed films before, working with Luca Guadagnino on Challengers, Queer, and the upcoming Artificial. To design for the big screen would hardly be a stretch for him.

The real question is more existential: Should Bond wear high fashion? To return to the idea of the 007 silhouette, that in itself is counterintuitive to Pattinson saving the world in one of Anderson’s menswear takes on the famous Dior Bar jacket, with its nipped waist and slightly flared hem. And yet in this brave new world of brand deals, anything is possible.

#3660. Titans' Jaylen Harrell, 24, Hospitalized After 'Serious Car Accident'

Tennessee Titans defensive end Jaylen Harrell has been hospitalized after a car crash.

“Yesterday, Jaylen Harrell was involved in a serious car accident that resulted in him being taken to the hospital in his hometown of Tampa, Florida,” a rep for the Titans told ESPN in a Saturday, November 21, statement. “We have been in constant communication with Jaylen’s family and are still working to gather more information.

Harrell, 24, had been a passenger in an Uber rideshare at the time of the accident, ESPN reported. No further details have been publicly shared.

The linebacker, who was selected by the Titans in the seventh round of the 2024 draft, has been on injured reserve at the start of the 2026-2027 NFL season after tearing his ACL in the preseason.

“I’m praying for Jaylen,” his teammate Kevin Winston Jr. told reporters during an August press conference. “I talked to him about it, having went through the same thing. I told him he’s gonna be just fine. I know Jaylen as a person, I told him I’m praying for him and best of luck with everything. I talked to him even before anything happened, just wishing the best and make sure he’s keeping his head high.”

The safety, 22, added, “He’s gonna come back better than ever. You know, a lot of the time, these ACL injuries when you’re dealing with guys that really care about their bodies and take care of themselves, they always come back stronger. I’m feeling that myself, so I’m excited for Jaylen and I’m praying for him, as well.”

Long before his injury, Harrell was focused on consistently improving his football skills.

“I feel like I’ve always had that prove-it mindset,” he told reporters in 2024. “Coming off a national championship team [in college], you get to the league, and nobody cares about that — you have to show you can do it on the biggest stage.”

Harrell continued at the time, “I always have belief in myself. I am always a hard worker, a go-get-it type dude. So, I feel like that is my mindset. I look at everything like: I’m a seventh-round rookie and I have to go get everything, ain’t nothing I’m going to get, I have to go earn everything, you feel me? I have to go attack each day, day by day.”

When Calls the Heart’s 13th season ended with a proposal amid the 2026 TV schedule, and fan have since been clamoring for more! Fan-favorite couple Elizabeth Thornton (Erin Krakow) and Nathan Grant (Kevin McGarry) finally got engaged on the long-running Hallmark drama, and Hope Valley is abuzz with wedding preparations. As filming for Season 14 begins to wrap up, the network has released a new look, and Hearties have a lot of thoughts in the aftermath of that wedding-centric trailer.

Just recently, Hallmark Channel surprised fans by releasing a new trailer for WCTH Season 14, which officially premieres this coming January. Naturally, the trailer centers on Elizabeth and Nathan’s much-anticipated nuptials, and how the town is preparing. The two characters seem to be content about their impending union couple, and the excitement is definitely building in Hope Valley:

A post shared by Hallmark Channel (@hallmarkchannel)

Elizabeth and Nathan’s engagement and subsequent wedding have been a long time coming. Viewers have witnessed quite a bit on the romance front, including the love triangle between Elizabeth, Nathan and Lucas (Chris McNally). The two have gone through a lot together and separately, and as someone who has been rooting for them for a while, I could not be happier that this is finally happening. And I’m not the only one. Plenty of Hearties took to the comments of the Instagram video to share their excitement, including user apeyberg, who loves this early Christmas present:

❤️ Oh. My. Goodness! Can't wait! Thank you so much Hallmark Channel! The BEST Christmas gift!

Given filming on When Calls the Heart's new season is nearly done and the show usually returns pretty early in a given year, this trailer being dropped now makes sense. However, now that the first trailer is out and we've seen glimpses of what's to come, the wait could become even more tougher. Still, pcmy01’s excitement is building:

The anticipation and excitement that’s building up inside ALL WCTH FANS right now is skyrocketing!!! I, we, can hardly hold it together. This is gonna be epic! 🙌🏾♥️🤩🔥🔥🔥🔥🔥

Ever since the Season 13 finale aired in March, I've personally found the wait for Season 14 to be tough, and I'm not sure this great new tease is going to make that easier for me. And, based on the comment shared by heartiefollower, this little promo is going to go a long way amid the wait:

I'm so glad this promo lasts for 20 minutes 😍

Meanwhile, along with Nathan and Elizabeth’s wedding, there is something else that fans can look forward to. Season 14 will mark the return of Lori Loughlin’s Abigail Stanton. It was announced last year that the Full House alum would be back in after exiting the show during Season 6. Fans got a glimpse of Abigail at the very end of the Season 13 finale when she officially returned to Hope Valley, and loriloughlinerinkrakowfan is excited to have her back:

So BEYOND happy to have our Abigail back!!! 🥹💕

The reveal of the premiere date also makes the prospect of the show's return feel much more real. mamazach_jackiez is looking forward to everything coming in Season 14, and I’m right there with them:

I can barely wait, so looking forward to this beautiful wedding and all season 14 brings!

Like so many others, I really hope the wait for When Calls the Heart's return won't be too bad. Hopefully, now that we’re getting into the holiday season, time will be moving a little bit quicker. That aside, though, I'm optimistic that the moment Nathan and Elizabeth finally say “I do” will be well worth the wait. On that note, WCTH Season 14 premieres on Sunday, January 3 at 8 p.m. ET on Hallmark Channel.

#3657. Pedro Almodóvar Didn’t Think He Could Write a Novel. But Once He Started, the “Story Began to Pour Out”

A woman who might, or might not, be Penélope Cruz stares down at us from the wall. For now, I’ll accept that it is Cruz because the image is on a poster for Broken Embraces, a 2009 film she starred in. My hesitation in believing it’s her, however, is because finding a resemblance between the woman on the poster and Cruz requires a lot of generosity. It’s as if the artist had painted her based on a detailed description he’d heard, but he’d never actually seen his subject onscreen. “We were given this in India,” explains Pedro Almodóvar’s brother, Agustín, the head and owner of El Deseo, the production company behind Almodóvar’s films. “Specialized artists still hand-paint their movie posters, and the results are images like this.” The work’s imperfections give it a charm that no poster created by AI could ever match.

This brings to mind one of the stories in Almodóvar’s first novel, The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes. It depicts a Blade Runner–style dystopian future where replicants, jaded by digital perfection, are fascinated by the rough edges of human culture. The book has just been published in Spain (it is scheduled to be published in the United States, in Spanish, in February 2027), following the release of Almodóvar’s latest film, Bitter Christmas (which will be in select US theaters on November 13, and released nationwide on November 25).

Both works have much in common: They are works of autofiction with protagonists—the filmmakers played by Bárbara Lennie and Leonardo Sbaraglia in the film, and a very multifaceted character named Flavio Guijarro in the book—who appear to be alternative versions of their creator. At the same time, they are clearly different from Almodóvar, like the difference between Cruz and the woman on the Indian movie poster.

I ask Almodóvar why he decided to recount Flavio’s story in the form of a novel rather than a movie, but he appears to have not heard my question and answers instead as if I’d asked him why it took him so long to publish a novel, which is undoubtedly much more interesting: “I think the reason I hadn’t written a novel until now was that I wasn’t sure I’d be able to, even though I’d wanted to write one since I was a young man. At first, however, I didn’t even know myself that this story would be a novel. I started with a simple anecdote about an acting coach and an actor, and that opened the floodgates; the story began to pour out. When it was already over 30 pages, I sent it to my editor. He told me there was a novel there and that I should keep going.”

The 77-year-old director from La Mancha poses in a jacket, polo shirt, pants, and sneakers by Loewe.

He will answer many other questions that I haven’t asked but should have: “I didn’t know, for example, that I’d include my story ‘Addiction,’ which is a little treat for fans that had already appeared in Pain and Glory. It was going to be a monologue that Carmen Machi would perform in a small theater, but I ended up giving it to Asier Etxeandia in that film. I also wrote Pain and Glory very quickly. And in it, I inserted, like little snippets, more pieces that I’d already written. For example, there’s another story, just five pages long, about a chance encounter with an actor with whom I’d had a very bad relationship in the past [Eusebio Poncela, who starred in Law of Desire 40 years ago] and with whom, in the story, I ended up doing heroin. In real life, the fact that he was using heroin while we were filming was the reason we had a falling out. Thanks to those preexisting elements, which fit into the story, I was able to write that movie so quickly. And the same is true of my new book. What defines it is a sense of absolute freedom.”

And maybe that sentence is, in the end, the answer to all my questions for Almodóvar.

Vanity Fair España: Is that sense of freedom why you decided to write a novel instead of a screenplay?

Pedro Almodóvar: In Bitter Christmas, Leonardo Sbaraglia’s character says he needs absolute freedom to work. Just like me throughout my entire career. That freedom feels more intense with a novel because it’s a format with which I have less experience. I’ve woven it together from different stories, but they all revolve around the protagonist and it’s been very satisfying. It wasn’t a whim: The book has the same rigor to it as everything else I do, but that freedom is deeply rooted in my style. That’s why I wrote it so quickly. Everything flowed naturally.

There is a tradition of using a novel as a container for many stories, as with Don Quixote or Jan Potocki’s The Manuscript Found in Saragossa. On the other hand, speaking of influences, it’s interesting that when you wrote your Patty Diphusa stories in 1983 [included in Patty Diphusa and Other Writings, published by Faber & Faber in 1992], Anita Loos and pornographic photo novels are influences that appear in the mix, but in The Man Who Only Wrote on Airplanes, you turn to, let’s say, more distinguished names: Henry James, Nabokov, and Colm Tóibín, who even appears as a character.

I’m not trying to compare myself to Cervantes or Potocki, but yes, that’s what the book is. That’s precisely why this novel can’t be adapted for the screen: You’d have to choose one part of it and develop it, but as it stands now, that wouldn’t be possible. Those earlier influences are still with me—Anita Loos is certainly among them—and they continue to inspire me with both specific phrases and broader themes. In the novel, I name authors who inspire me and with whom I connect organically, such as Joan Didion and Virginia Woolf. But Patty and Flavio have something in common: a sense of urgency that drives them to write at a breakneck pace, out of a physiological need. Neither of them sleeps much, though in Patty’s case it’s because she can’t stop doing cocaine. Beyond that, other differences set them apart, including the differences between what life was like in the ’80s and what it’s like now.

What sort of differences are there, and where are they most apparent?

Take sex, for example. Patty Diphusa is an archetype of the 1980s, a time of absolute freedom in Spain, and her character can only be understood in the context of the utterly carefree and hedonistic lifestyle we led back then. If she sucks a guy's dick in a bathroom, she’ll then record her wild thoughts because she considers herself a sort of philosopher of eroticism. Although Flavio is a very free-spirited person, just like the book itself, he belongs to another era and another generation. Here, sex is part of a love story, and his attitude toward it is very different. I devote less space to the erotic scenes in this book because I assume people already know what it’s like to sleep with someone.

Almodóvar, in another room at El Deseo’s headquarters, wearing a Louis Vuitton jacket and a Prada knit polo shirt.

You’ve argued on different occasions that in the 1980s, many people in Spain chose that hedonistic and seemingly frivolous lifestyle as a reaction to the previous era, and that this was a political statement. Now we see a new generation adopting a different kind of stance. For example, all across Europe, people are taking to the streets to demand their right to housing and decent living conditions, and there’s not much frivolity in that. How do you interpret this change?

I completely empathize with and support the people filling the streets. They are demanding fundamental rights that are enshrined in the Spanish constitution and which are now in jeopardy: housing, health care, and education. I went to the encampment on the Puerta del Sol [in Madrid] only a few times, because I was in New York presenting Bitter Christmas at the New York Film Festival and also because I think a famous person doesn’t really fit in at these demonstrations—if we go, we distort the spirit of it. But I did go, and I bought them food because that’s what I thought they’d need, even though they told me they’d be better off with some tables. I don’t just support their initiative; I’m glad it happened. One thing I’d heard about young people, a generation I don’t know much about, was from a news article that said that 25% of young Spaniards wouldn’t mind living under a dictatorship like Franco’s. I shuddered. What happened in the Puerta del Sol shows that there’s a whole crowd of young people beyond those who go to Ferraz to pray the rosary [since November 2023, a group of Catholic protesters has gathered daily to pray outside the headquarters of the PSOE, Spain’s socialist party, on Madrid’s Calle Ferraz]. They aren’t rich, and they don’t have their lives figured out; they can’t work in the professions they studied to pursue, and they don’t earn enough money to buy homes. That’s terrifying. And the political parties have shown their true colors when it comes to housing. Of course, the PSOE is late to the game with the so-called Maricarmen decrees [a series of measures named after Maricarmen Abascal, whose eviction from her home and subsequent death in October galvanized activists], but at least it has reacted. The starkly different reactions from the Partido Popular [Popular Party] and Vox [center-right and far-right parties, respectively] already tell you what they think about this issue.

Would you agree today with that line from Gloria Muñoz in The Flower of My Secret: “With so much reality, the country’s ready to explode”?

She was talking in literary terms, but it’s true that this phrase has taken on a life of its own over time and has spilled over into other areas. The same thing has happened to another phrase: “A woman is more authentic the more she resembles the person she has dreamed of becoming,” as Agrado said in All About My Mother. It was a line written for a transgender woman, and one that makes perfect sense for her. But now it can be understood in relation to any kind of character: It speaks to authenticity, to staying true to oneself and to one’s own dreams. In the case of young people in our country, we’re talking about a social reality. The country has changed a lot, and we’re very polarized—though France is even worse off than Spain. Europe is in very bad shape overall. The kind of news coverage being produced plays a major role in this rise of the far right. Since the images promoted by the right are so jarring and sensationalist, TV stations pick up on them, and in doing so, they’re effectively promoting figures like Vito Quiles [a far-right activist and influencer]. Damn it, don’t put Vito Quiles on TV—it’s better if we don’t even know where he is or what he’s doing!

Are you particularly concerned about the attention that the far right is getting?

People like [Santiago] Abascal [president of the Vox political party] and [Javier]Milei [president of Argentina] want to do away with the state. Milei, the biggest loudmouth of them all, even aims to destroy the state from within the state itself, which is diabolical. I cite Milei as an example because he says so himself. And on top of that, people elect him for that very reason: He’s someone who has come to power democratically, just like [Donald] Trump. So we’re putting the tools of democracy in the hands of someone whose main goal is to destroy it. Furthermore, in a world so polarized—and with a far right that has no qualms about calling itself fascist—the emergence of AI creates a perfect storm.

One of the stories in your book is, in fact, a dystopian tale inspired by Blade Runner, in which large corporations with shadowy agendas seek to create a less human world. You have contributed so much to human creativity. Are you concerned about how that creativity is being taken over by AI?

I’m always open to change. It’s necessary for society to move forward. But I think the encroachment of AI on human agency is terrible. They should start regulating it now. I’m concerned about the jobs it will replace and also the synthetic culture it will create. In fact, a synthetic culture based on data already exists, and it lacks a soul. The genesis of a screenplay must be human, because AI doesn’t have the sense of doubt, the patience, or the capacity for stories to build up layers of meaning, as in Talk to Her and Bad Education. We need a society that cares about culture, promotes it, and supports it, and not a soulless culture focused only on the immediate. I haven’t used AI creatively, nor do I really know how to. But I’m concerned that we’re now unable to tell whether an image is real or not, given the level of perfection this technology has reached. And moreover, behind it all are very powerful people who know no limits.

On another topic, standards of beauty have changed, with cosmetic surgery and fillers now widely prevalent. For someone who places such importance on the expressions of actors that must also be a cause for concern.

Well, I wouldn’t mind if an actor in one of my movies had had plastic surgery. For example, I wouldn’t turn down Nicole Kidman for that reason—she’s not only a great actor, but she has also had plastic surgery, and she looks better than ever. Because, these days, actors who’ve had plastic surgery are part of the landscape. It’s so common that you no longer have to explain that a character has had it done; it’s accepted as a matter of course. What’s more, cosmetic surgery has advanced so much that high-profile figures who’ve had work done—like Donatella Versace, Lindsay Lohan, or Nicole Kidman herself—have completely erased the signs of their previous procedures with splendid results. [Editor’s note: Lindsay Lohan has denied having a facelift, while Kidman has never confirmed undergoing any plastic surgery.] The big problem is that, if you make films set in the past, you can’t cast women with plastic surgery or lip fillers; it would be anachronistic, just like putting a piece of furniture from the 1980s in a film about the Spanish Civil War. But it’s true that in my films, plastic surgery hasn’t usually been an option, for aesthetic reasons. Fortunately, there will always be people like Frances McDormand and Carmen Maura. We need older women who look their age.

What interests me most about your new novel is the protagonist’s relationship with an actor, Alez Mazado—a sex symbol who isn’t very intelligent but has a certain natural talent and is open to being molded. Flavio is his Pygmalion. There’s even an explicit reference to Hitchcock’s film Vertigo, which also features that kind of relationship. Do you often have that kind of dynamic with your actors?

I’m like Jimmy Stewart in Vertigo: With actors, I get involved in their hair, lip color, outfits—everything. When I watched Vertigo for the umpteenth time, I thought that character was a director: “He knows exactly what he wants,” they tell him when he takes Kim Novak to try on outfits at a store. The actors I work with and I have adapted to each other, just like in a marriage—in my films, they speak differently; the actors themselves say so. Aitana Sánchez-Gijón told me that she felt she could do anything after playing her role in Bitter Christmas. But I work differently with each actor. With Penélope, for example, I rehearse a lot, and the more we rehearse, the better she gets; then I shoot many takes, and the 10th one is better than the third. And if I can shoot 12, even better. But others don’t like to rehearse, like Antonio Banderas, because he’s a different kind of actor. He has extraordinary intuition and instinct. I don’t need to talk to him as much or push him so hard.

People talk about Los Javis [the moniker for actors turned directors Javier Ambrossi and Javier Calvo] as your natural heirs, in the wake of the success of La Bola Negra, which you coproduced through El Deseo. Do you think they will continue your creative legacy?

They definitely treat me like their mentor. They know entire films of mine by heart, even lines that I don’t remember. They’ve been deeply influenced by my films, just as I’ve been influenced by [Luis García] Berlanga, [Rafael] Azcona, [Luis] Buñuel, and [Carlos] Saura. Even if you don’t want to admit it, everyone has role models. I find it flattering, but to say they’re my heirs is to minimize their work. They have a style all their own. In fact, if I were to write the screenplay for La Bola Negra, it would be very different. I don’t feel like their father. I take responsibility for my films and nothing else.

How do you view their film’s unstoppable run at the awards and at the box office?

Los Javis are the big thing right now. Their film is going to be the highest-grossing Spanish movie of all time, although I don’t remember how much The Last Torch Song (1957), starring Sara Montiel, made back in the day. At El Deseo, we’ve had two fantastic years—first with Oliver Laxe’s film [Sirāt], which we also coproduced, and now this one. And I hope the Javis can keep on going and make it through the rest of their promotional tour and then the awards season. From my experience as an Oscar nominee, I know the best moment isn’t when they call your name, but when the ceremony ends. That’s when your life is your own again—whether to start on the next project or simply sleep if that’s what you prefer.

Have you shared that experience with the Javis? Do you give them advice?

Just yesterday I texted Javier Ambrossi, and he told me they’ve already had enough. And they have no idea what’s still in store for them! We’ll meet next week, and I’ll explain it all to him. At the Oscars, they’re the favorites in the best-international-feature-film category; they’re a sure thing. Although I experienced that curse of being the front-runner when Women on the Verge of a Nervous Breakdown was the favorite and then Pelle the Conqueror ended up winning—a film no one even remembers now. But anyway, everyone now expects La Bola Negra to be nominated in other categories as well, which is historic for our film industry. It’s great for us.

On a recent podcast, one of the actors from La Bola Negra, Yenesi, described the film as Federico García Lorca fan fiction—which is actually quite fitting, since its entire narrative is built on elements related to Lorca’s life and writings. Roland Barthes had already spoken of the death of the author, and Eugenio d’Ors famously said, “There is no true originality outside tradition. Everything that is not tradition is plagiarism.”

I’ve written that phrase down! I read it in one of [journalist and writer Francisco] Umbral’s columns; I suppose he got it from d’Ors.

In other words, Umbral appropriated it for himself, and in doing so, he proved its enduring relevance.

It’s inevitable that the things you like will influence your work. And the things you hate too. When you write, you have a general idea of the story, but as you develop it, what you create is rooted in things that are part of your life. And your life always resembles the things you’ve seen before. I’m fascinated by the phenomenon of fan fiction because of its contradictory nature; it’s a miracle that an entire culture has developed around this phenomenon, which exists outside the mainstream market yet at the same time feeds off the most mainstream works, such as Star Trek or Star Wars. Fan fiction is a declaration of love for the original and proof that great stories never end: There will always be someone to continue them. Just as people don’t die as long as there’s someone who remembers them.

Of course I have to ask you, with the promotional tour for Bitter Christmas coming to an end, what are you working on next?

Well, it was going to be a comedy, but after I finished it, even though I was 90% passionate about it, I realized there was something about the supporting characters that I didn’t like. So I’ve put it on hold, as I’ve done before with other projects. And now I’m writing something else. I’m well into it, but I can’t say anything. They’ll kill me if I do. It’ll be based on a book, and we’re currently working out the rights. This one will have plenty of humor too. Because I know for sure that, after Bitter Christmas, I don’t want to talk about myself anymore. I need different characters. And humor too.

Is there any movie you wish you’d made but that’s missing from your filmography?

There are several recent films I would have loved to have made. For example, Drive My Car by Ryusuke Hamaguchi and Anatomy of a Fall by Justine Triet. Or Sentimental Value by Joachim Trier. I mean, I should have made that movie! It has everything: the cinema, a house, a father and his daughters. Everything.

Should we just accept, by the way, that you won’t make your own movie about the Spanish Civil War? Or was Parallel Mothers already your take on it?

When I read Cosamala, Alana S. Portero’s latest book, I really wanted to adapt it. But it’s such a wonderful work of literature that translating it into images would greatly diminish the wonder and surprise of her writing. If the book proves anything, it’s that Alana is a tremendous writer. I’d have to find another angle from which to tell the story of the civil war. But I do want to do it.

#3656. Here's What We Know About Amazon's Black Friday and Cyber Monday 2026 Sales

Gone are the days when holiday sales had a firm beginning and end. These days, if you're not scouring the internet weeks before the actual date of the event, you will miss out on deals. Black Friday is no exception. Amazon released its official Black Friday and Cyber Monday plans for its sale, but there's plenty that's discounted already, many reaching or matching their lowest price ever.

Amazon is treating Black Friday and Cyber Monday like one long sale. The official sale kicks off at 12:01 a.m. PST on Nov. 19 and runs through Nov. 30.

Yes, you will need to be a Prime Member to shop the exclusive sales during Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Prime membership starts at $14.99 per month. While only you can decide if buying a yearly Prime membership is worth it for you, remember you can always sign up and then cancel your Prime membership once the sale is over: Amazon offers a free 30-day trial, so you can shop during both Black Friday and Cyber Monday before canceling without being charged. Here's how to sign up for a Prime account and all of the benefits that come with it.

This year, Amazon says you can expect "millions" of deals across categories like electronics, beauty, fashion, toys, home, and more from brands like Medicube, Le Creuset, HP, Google, and Stanley. There will also be limited-time deals of up to 60% off that will drop at midnight and 8 a.m. PST on both Black Friday and Cyber Monday. Here are some other deals Amazon says you can expect:

As stated already, just because the sale hasn't officially started, that doesn't mean you can't find great deals. You can follow all of our Black Friday coverage here. Here are some of the best deals we've found so far:

As far as volume, Amazon will usually beat Walmart and Best Buy in most cases, but most flagship products will likely be the same price in all three retailers. However, don't sleep on Walmart or Best Buy. There are usually a couple of surprising deals that beat Amazon (although Amazon usually matches the deal eventually).

The other major retailers doing sales are Best Buy, Target, and Walmart. Currently, Best Buy is offering one of the largest Cyber Week sales, with new deals available every Friday. Target has some week-long deals and a Deal of the Day. Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Cyber Monday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026.

If this will be your first Black Friday shopping at Amazon, there are some basic things you need to know about Amazon sales:

You can share your Prime membership with family members using Amazon Family.

You can set price alerts for products you want, and your Alexa devices can notify you when they go on sale.

There are usually some invite-only deals that you can sign up for.

But if you only take one bit of advice for shopping on Amazon, let it be this one: Don't buy anything you weren't going to buy anyway. A good way to make sure you do this is by making a list of the products you do want, and only having eyes for those.

Black Friday used to be bigger for major retailers and more expensive tech and appliances, while Cyber Monday was better for cheaper tech and gave smaller businesses a chance to compete online. Nowadays, though, the distinction is almost meaningless. Every major retailer will offer sales on both days, and the smart move is to know what you want, do your research, or refer to guides like our Black Friday and Cyber Monday coverage that have done all the vetting for you.

Nowadays, both large retailers and small businesses compete for Black Friday shoppers, so you can expect practically every store to run sales through Monday, Nov. 30, 2026. The “best” sales depend on your needs, but in general, the biggest discounts tend to come from larger retailers who can afford lower prices: Think places like Amazon, Walmart, Target, Best Buy, and Home Depot. You can find all the best sales from major retailers on our Black Friday coverage.

In short, yes, Black Friday still offers discounts that you're less likely to see throughout the rest of the year. If there’s something you want to buy, or you’re shopping for gifts, it’s a good time to look for discounts on what you need, especially tech sales, home improvement supplies, and fitness tech.

#3655. PlayStation Plus Is Losing More Games, But One Departure Stings The Most

New arrivals are landing in the PlayStation Plus Game Catalog this month, but at the same time, you can also expect a few departures from that gaming library. Fortunately, the number of games leaving soon are on the smaller side, as there'll be only three exits in total. Unfortunately, one of those games that you're running out of time to play through the Game Catalog is a massive and pretty fun fantasy title, so get those hours in while you can.

PlayStation Plus Game Catalog games leaving soon

  • Granblue Fantasy Relink
  • Somerville
  • Fade to Silence

This month's biggest departure is Granblue Fantasy Relink, a massive fantasy game with a storybook art style, cinematic boss fights, and a large roster of characters who all possess unique abilities to master. First released in February 2024, Granblue Fantasy Relink is built around real-time combat and flashy team-up mechanics, making for a visually striking experience overall. While the story isn't much to write home about, it's the gameplay and worldbuilding where this Granblue spin-off shines, and it got even better earlier this year with the Endless Ragnarok expansion.

In comparison, Somerville is a story-rich puzzle game that's oozing atmosphere with its slick art direction, and Fade to Silence is a single-player and co-op survival-crafting adventure set in a post-apocalyptic world that is feeling the chill of an eternal winter.

While the Game Catalog is going to be a little poorer without those three titles, it is getting some great games this month. Death Stranding 2: On the Beach is the headline act, and it'll be joined by several more titles like Atomfall, Dragon Quest 3 HD-2D Remake, and Like a Dragon: Pirate Yakuza in Hawaii. All PlayStation Plus subscribers can also grab a trio of freebies between now and November 30: Dead Island 2, Tomb Raider 4-6 Remastered, and Monster Train 2.
